name: Julian of Norwich
knownFor: A recluse at Norwich who wrote down the showings she received in May 1373, in a sickness she thought would kill her. Her book survives in a shorter and a longer version. Both hold the words "all shall be well". She wrote it for her fellow Christians, "for I would God were known", while refusing to be called a teacher.
dates: Her book dates the showings to 13 May 1373, when she was "thirty years old and a half". Grace Warrack, who edited the long version in 1901, reckons her birth about the end of 1342. A copyist calls her still alive in 1413, as Dundas Harford, who first printed the short version, reads him. Francis Blomefield, an eighteenth-century historian of Norfolk, read 1442.
place: Norwich, where the copyist calls her a recluse. Harford places her cell at the church of St Julian, Norwich. Blomefield, quoted by Warrack, places an anchorage in the east part of its churchyard, in the parish of Conisford.
role: Anchoress, or recluse, living shut in a cell; writer of the Revelations of Divine Love

keyWorks.title: Revelations of Divine Love (the long version)
keyWorks.about: the showings and her later thought on them. She writes of an answer that came "fifteen years after, and more". She also writes that she was taught inwardly "twenty years after the time of the Shewing, save three months". Grace Warrack printed it in modern spelling from the Sloane manuscript in 1901

keyWorks.title: The short version (Comfortable Words for Christ's Lovers)
keyWorks.about: a shorter text of the showings, under a copyist's heading that names her. Dundas Harford printed it for the first time, after the British Museum bought the manuscript at Lord Amherst's sale in 1909

traces: Serenus de Cressy, a Benedictine, first printed her book in 1670, Warrack says, by leave of the abbot of Lambspring. It was printed again in 1843.

Warrack compares two manuscripts of the long version, the Sloane copy in the British Museum and a copy now at Paris. The Paris copyist closes with a prayer for the soul of Julian, anchoress of Norwich.
A scribe of the Sloane copy adds a warning. Readers are not to take one thing to their liking and leave another, for that, he says, is what heretics do.

Tersteegen gave a long extract from her book in his Auserlesene Beschreibungen Heiliger Seelen, third edition 1784, Warrack notes. He said he had seen a manuscript of it in the library of Pierre Poiret, who died in 1719.
Henry Collins published a modernized version from the Sloane manuscript in 1877, Warrack notes.
remembered: Pierre Poiret, a writer on mystical theology, listed her book in his catalogue of mystical writers in 1702. Warrack says he marked her name with his sign of greatness. In modern words, his Latin entry reads taught by God, profound, ecstatic.
Cressy's title of 1670 calls her "Mother Juliana", an anchoress of Norwich. Warrack thinks Cressy probably began that name, and says the old name was Julian.
Blomefield, quoted by Warrack, says the anchoress Lady Julian was a strict recluse in 1393, with two servants. She was "esteemed one of the greatest holiness", he writes.
Evelyn Underhill, introducing Frances Comper's edition of Rolle's Fire of Love in 1914, calls her book "perhaps the finest flower of English religious literature".
Harford, the first editor of the short version, writes that she "deserves to rank high amongst the great mystics of the world".

uncertain: Her name and last trace. Her book never names her. A copyist's heading on the short version calls her Julian, a recluse at Norwich, still alive. Dundas Harford reads its year as 1413. Francis Blomefield read 1442, and Grace Warrack followed him in 1901. Harford calls this a curious mistake that misled all later writers.

Whether she was Julian Lampet. Dame Julian Lampet was an anchoress at Carrow, the Benedictine nunnery by Norwich. Wills listed by Walter Rye in 1889, whom Warrack cites, name her from 1427 to 1478. A Bury will of 1463 leaves her twenty pence. J. B. Dalgairns, a priest of the Oratory, writing in 1870, thought it most probable that the two were one woman, who lived to a hundred. Warrack calls that surely an impossibility.
When she was born. Her book gives her age, thirty and a half, in May 1373. Warrack reckons the end of 1342 and Harford about 1342. Evelyn Underhill gives 1343.

When she died. J. B. Dalgairns says she appears to have died in 1443, and so lived to be a hundred. He gives no ground for the year. Underhill, in her edition of Hilton's Scale of 1923, gives her years as 1343 to about 1413.

How learned she was. In Warrack's text she calls herself "a simple creature unlettered". The Sloane manuscript says she knew no letter, which Warrack glosses as unskilled in letters. The Sloane copy's title calls her one "who could not read a Letter". In the short version she calls herself "a woman unlearned".

Her schooling and vows. Warrack writes that she would probably be sent to the Benedictine nuns of Carrow for her schooling. She thinks it "most likely" that Julian was made a nun there. Harford says no outside evidence for her life can be relied on.

Which version came first. Harford holds that the long version was expanded from the short one, over twenty years of thought. He notes that others had suggested the short one was cut down from the long.
